tool.name: RepeatingShapes

summary.para: Tessellates an area of interest with hexagons, squares, triangles or rectangles (brick courses with an adjustable offset), or lays out sampling points or circles in a square or triangular arrangement -- at any orientation angle. Sizes are given in real units (hectares, acres, feet, miles, ...) and converted to the output coordinate system automatically; typing any one measure fills the others. The area of interest is a polygon layer (selection honored, holes respected) or a plain extent; edge shapes are kept whole when they intersect the area, kept only when their center is inside, or clipped. Geographic data is computed in an automatic equal-area projection so cell areas are exact. A modernized port of Jeff Jenness's classic Repeating Shapes extension. Works at every license level.

tool.usage: A modernized port of the classic Repeating Shapes extension (Jenness Enterprises), with the same eight patterns and every size measure of the original dialogs -- hexagons by area / edge / width (across flats) / diameter (corner to corner); squares by area / edge; triangles by area / edge / height; rectangles by Edge 1 (width) + Edge 2 (height) + percent brick offset (cumulative per course: 50 = running bond, 33 = staircase); circles by area / radius / diameter / circumference plus a center spacing (default: touching); points by center spacing. Typing a value into any one box fills the others automatically (enter a square area of 4 square miles and the edge length becomes 2 miles), exactly as the original dialogs did. Units: sizes carry real units. Area units: square meters, hectares, square kilometers, square feet, acres, square miles. Length units: meters, kilometers, feet, miles. Choosing an area unit snaps the length unit to its natural partner (square meters or hectares -> meters; square kilometers -> kilometers; square miles -> miles; acres or square feet -> feet). Everything is converted to the output coordinate system internally -- no need to look up its units. Geographic data gets a mathematically honest treatment: truly regular equal-area tessellations of a curved surface are impossible (Euler's formula forces 12 pentagons into any hexagon-dominant tiling of a sphere -- the soccer ball), so something must flex. This tool keeps cell areas exact by computing in an automatic Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centered on the area of interest (built on the input's own datum) and writing the results back in the input geographic coordinate system; shape regularity absorbs the distortion, which grows only as (distance/2R)^2 -- about 0.15% at 500 km from the center, invisible at management scales. Continental or global tessellation belongs to discrete global grid systems (ISEA3H, H3), which accept those 12 pentagons in exchange for global coverage; the tool warns when the area of interest approaches that scale. The orientation angle rotates the whole lattice counterclockwise about the area's center. By symmetry, hexagons and triangles repeat every 60 degrees, squares every 90. Edge behavior: the classic behavior keeps every whole shape that intersects the area of interest (sampling designs usually want complete cells); alternatively keep only shapes whose center falls inside, or clip the border shapes to the area (a true partition -- edge cells then differ in area). The Extent geoprocessing environment overrides the area used for generation. Speed: the original built every shape one at a time and then deleted the extras feature-by-feature; this version generates the whole lattice numerically, filters it in bulk, and only writes the shapes that survive -- typically orders of magnitude faster. dialogReference.para: The pattern to generate. Sample images of every pattern are on the tool help page (the ? button).

param.name: boundary
param.displayname: Area of interest (optional -- polygons enclose the area; lines or points keep the shapes that touch them; else the extent below)

dialogReference.para: The area of interest. Polygons enclose the area to fill (multiple polygons unioned, holes respected, selection honored). Line or point features instead select: every shape touching a line (hexagons over a river) or containing a point (observation locations) is kept whole; for point patterns, the point's lattice tile plays the shape's role. Leave blank to use the extent parameter instead.

param.name: extent
param.displayname: Extent (used when no polygon is given; the Extent environment overrides both)

dialogReference.para: A plain rectangular area of interest, used when no polygon is given. The Extent geoprocessing environment overrides both.
The area of one hexagon, square, triangle or circle, in the area units below. Give any ONE size measure; the rest fill in automatically.

Units for the shape area. Choosing one snaps the length units to the natural partner: square meters / hectares -> meters; square kilometers -> kilometers; square miles -> miles; acres / square feet -> feet.

param.name: linear_units
param.displayname: Units for all lengths, spacings and radii

dialogReference.para: Units for every length box: edge, width, height, diameter, radius, circumference and spacing.
The edge (side) length of a hexagon, triangle or square.

param.name: width
param.displayname: Width (hexagon width across flats, or rectangle Edge 1)

dialogReference.para: The hexagon's width across the flats (flat side to flat side), or the rectangle's Edge 1.
The triangle's height (base to apex), or the rectangle's Edge 2.
The hexagon's corner-to-corner diameter, or the circle's diameter.

param.name: spacing
param.displayname: Spacing between point or circle centers

dialogReference.para: The center-to-center distance between points or circles. For circles it defaults to twice the radius (touching circles).

param.name: offset_pct
param.displayname: Brick offset, percent of Edge 1 (rectangles; 50 = running bond)

dialogReference.para: How far each course of rectangles shifts relative to the course below, as a percent of Edge 1: 50 = running bond (bricks), 33 = staircase, 0 = aligned columns.
Rotates the whole lattice counterclockwise, in degrees, about the area's center. Hexagons and triangles repeat every 60 degrees, squares every 90.
What happens to shapes at the area's edge:

bulletList.bullet_item: Keep whole shapes intersecting the area (the classic behavior).
Keep shapes whose center is inside the area.

dialogReference.para: Applies to polygon or extent areas of interest; with line or point features there is no inside, so touching shapes are always kept whole.
The output feature class (points for the point patterns, polygons otherwise) with Cell_ID and -- for polygons -- a geodesic-hectares Area_Ha field.

scriptExample.title: Repeating Shapes example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: 100-hectare hexagons over a study area, whole cells kept.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path arcpy.jenness.RepeatingShapes( shape_type="Hexagons", boundary=r"D:\data\study.gdb\study_area", area=100.0, area_units="Hectares", orientation=15.0, edge_policy="Keep whole shapes intersecting the area (original)", out_fc=r"D:\data\study.gdb\hex_100ha")
